zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after the independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). The scan, not the lexical index or generated kana hints, determines the transcription.

lines.note: Suibocu combines water and wood, here glossed as water and firewood. The scan supports Mizzu rather than OCR Mzzu.
The example describes a place plentiful in water and firewood. The printed tacusanna is retained rather than replaced with a modern predicative construction.

runs.text: lugar he abundante de agoa, & lenha.

lines.note: Completes the Portuguese example as a place abundant in water and firewood. This closes the entry anticipated by the preceding page's catchword.

runs.text: Perda por muita agoa, & perda cau-

lines.note: Suican covers damage from too much water and another cause given below. Muita corrects OCR mutra; cau- begins cauſada.
Completes the second cause as severe drought. The entry thus pairs water damage and drought damage rather than treating the second phrase as more flooding.

runs.text: Hum vestido delgado que vſão nos

lines.note: This Suican is a light garment used in performances. The clothing sense is distinct from the preceding disaster term.
Completes the statement that the garment is used in dramatic performances or plays. The short Portuguese noun is retained as its own physical row.
Suicaqi is an open fence or hedge resembling bars or latticework. The source's consonant spelling is not modernized.
Suicazzura is described as a climbing plant suitable for a trellis. The double zz is preserved without imposing a modern botanical identification.
Suichicu is green bamboo, paraphrased by midori no take. The Portuguese canas supplies the plant category in the source's terminology.
Suichoo is a waterbird, paraphrased by mizzu-tori. The scan supports Suichô and Mizzutori, not the OCR's garbled forms; the Portuguese comparison continues below.
Completes marreca and adds adem, giving duck-like waterbirds as comparators. The scan supports the continuous word adem rather than OCR a dem.
Suichoo is a green curtain, paraphrased by midori no tobari. The caron distinguishes this printed form from the preceding waterbird entry's circumflex.
The Portuguese extends the description to rich, lustrous hanging fabrics. Suichǒ begins the compound example on the next row.
The example refers to decoration with such hangings and carpets. Alcatifas is supported by the visible f and its Portuguese meaning, correcting OCR alcatiſas.
Completes the ornamental description with rich carpets or crimson coverlets. The historical carmeſim is preserved.
Suichuu means within the water. The scan has the doubled zz in Mizzuno, correcting the single-z OCR form.
This homograph means in the midst of sleep. The phrase nemuri no uchi distinguishes it from the water compound despite identical printed headwords.
Suicocu pairs water and rice. The Portuguese gives the two components directly before the abstaining example.
Suicoku wo tatsu means cutting off food and drink. The first part of the Portuguese gloss concerns abstaining from eating.
Adds drinking to the abstention, completing the example. The short continuation is preserved as printed.
Suicomi is sucking in and swallowing. The printed circumflex and ôda principal part are retained rather than replaced by a modern inflection.
Completes the explanation as swallowing by suction. The repeated engulir and the alternative introduced by l are part of the printed gloss.

runs.text: Couſa apetitoſa que ſe deita em algũ

lines.note: Suicuchi is an appetizing ingredient added to broth. The scan supports Couſa apetitoſa, correcting two malformed OCR words.

runs.text: caldo pera lhe dar mais ſabor.

lines.note: Completes the purpose: giving the broth more flavor. The row is physically indented and has been restored as a continuation in the Markdown placement.
Suidai is the element of water. The note follows the source's elemental terminology without importing a modern chemical sense.
Suidoo is a waterway, paraphrased by mizu no michi. The damaged initial M in Mizzuno corrects OCR Vizzuno.
Suifa combines water and waves. The Japanese paraphrase and Portuguese gloss agree on the two components.
Suifai concerns decline or ruin. The scan and the decline-related paraphrase support f in the headword rather than OCR r.
Completes the alternative sense of falling apart or being undone. This closes the decline entry.
Suifen is the water's edge, paraphrased by mizu no hotori. The following sentence illustrates the waterside setting.
Suifen ni natsu nashi says there is no summer at the water's edge. The scan corrects Soifen and restores the word division before natçu; borda corrects OCR berda.
Completes the statement that there is no summer or summer heat there. The source's proverbial or figurative wording is reported, not asserted as a climatic fact.
Suifin is a plant growing in water, paraphrased as floating water-grass. The entry is retained without imposing a species-level identification.
Completes the water-plant definition. The printed joining of na and agoa is preserved.
Suigin means dust or small particles on water, paraphrased by mizu no chiri. It is distinct from the water-deity entry Suijin in the other column.
The example says dust on water is easy to brush away. The Portuguese adverb is divided after Facil with a visible stop-like mark, retained rather than silently converted to a hyphen.

runs.text: mente ſe ſacode o poo da agoa.

lines.note: Completes facilmente and explains brushing the dust off water. The scan has poo, with two o letters, rather than the OCR's po.

runs.text: Matarſe botandoſe viuo no mar, ou

lines.note: Suigiǒ is defined as death by deliberately entering the sea or river. The note reports the historical dictionary's meaning; the printed caron is retained.
Completes the water setting and gives the compound with suru. Enlarged second-pass inspection distinguishes two medial r types in Morrer, correcting the draft's Morer.
Completes the gloss as dying in that manner. This closes the entry and is not part of the following intoxication term.
Suigo means after intoxication, paraphrased by yei no nochi. The historical Japanese yei form is preserved.
The example concerns urging someone to drink again after becoming drunk. The Portuguese translation begins with the divided Depois.

runs.text: is da bebedice tornar a fazer beber.

lines.note: Completes Depois and explains making or encouraging the person to drink again after intoxication. The odd physical division Depo-/is is preserved.
This Suigua means lying asleep, paraphrased by nemuri fusu. The scan corrects OCR Saigua; the printed stop-like division after dor is retained.
Completes dormindo, sleeping. The short continuation closes the sleep-related homograph.
The next Suigua means lying down drunk, paraphrased by yoi fusu. It is distinguished from the preceding entry by the explanation, not by a different headword spelling.
Completes the intoxication description with the printed tomado o vinho. No d is supplied to regularize it to tomado do vinho; the source's unusual wording remains visible.
Suiguen, paraphrased as minacami, is a water source or headwater. The Portuguese describes a spring of water.
Suiguet is the moon reflected in water, literally mizzuno tçuqi. The Portuguese explanation continues with the water on the next physical line.
This completes the moon's reflection seen in water. It belongs to Suiguet rather than starting a new entry.
Suiguin is mercury, with mizzucane as the Japanese equivalent. Azougue is the Portuguese name for mercury, not a reference to ordinary water.
Suiguio combines water and fish, explicitly unpacked as mizzu and vuo. The following example develops their inseparable relationship into a comparison for friendship.

The expression means to feel affection like the relationship of fish and water. The Portuguese begins 'to love one another, or'; the faint initial vowel in ou is read with its visible rounded outline and the continuation.
This completes the alternative gloss, to have friendship like fish and water. The comparison explains the preceding Japanese expression rather than defining another compound.
Suiguiǔ is a water buffalo. The brief Portuguese gloss Bufara is retained without replacing its historical form with a modern zoological name.
This Suijin is the deity of water, paraphrased as mizzuno cami. Cami is a Japanese word embedded in the otherwise Portuguese explanation and is marked for optional typeface review.

runs.text: O perguntar, ou inquirir per conjeituras.

lines.note: A separate homonymous Suijin denotes questioning or inquiry by conjecture. The scan supports conjeituras rather than the OCR's compeituras; historical per is retained.
Here Suijin means a drunken person, with yôta fito as the Japanese paraphrase. The alternative Portuguese expression is divided toma-do across the physical line break.
The first do completes tomado and the second introduces vinho: a man overcome by wine. The two adjacent occurrences are grammatically distinct and should not be deduplicated.

Suimen denotes sleeping, with the verb nemuri, u supplied as its Japanese equivalent. The headword's final n and dormir's first r are weak in the print but distinguishable; the example continues after Sui-.
This completes Suimen ſuru, to sleep. The visible final consonant of men is n, not the OCR's u.
This homonymous Suimen means the surface of water, literally mizzuno vomote. The Portuguese noun is completed by its complement on the next line.
Dagoa completes 'surface of water.' Its joined historical spelling is retained rather than divided or supplied with an apostrophe.
A third Suimen denotes a drunken face, paraphrased as yeyeru vomote. The Portuguese clearly includes the first b of bebado, which the draft omitted.
This separate Suimen is glossed as a silk material, Cangas de ſeda. The historical material name is retained without replacing it with a conjectured modern textile term.
Suimeô is a sleeping cat, explicitly nemuru neco. The circumflex on the headword and the Portuguese division dor-mindo are retained.
This completes dormindo, sleeping. It closes the gloss of the preceding cat entry and has no independent Japanese headword.
Suimet denotes decline and destruction, paraphrased with votoroye foroburu. The scan supports both the initial Sui- and Danificarſe; the draft's Srimet and Danifcarſe lose meaningful letters.
The Portuguese adds destruction to the preceding notion of damage or decline. It completes the same entry for Suimet.
Suimô literally involves blowing hair, as qeuo fuqu explains. The example names a sword whose exceptional sharpness is described over the following two lines.

runs.text: Eſpada que corta, ou leua os cabelinhos, que

lines.note: The sword cuts or takes away small hairs. The word is cabelinhos, not the OCR's cabelmnhos, and the relative clause continues on the next physical line.

runs.text: ſe ſoprão por cima. i, que corta muito bẽ.

lines.note: The hairs are blown over the blade; the explanation concludes that it cuts very well. The row is visibly indented and continues the preceding gloss, so its placement is corrected without changing its ID.
Suimon is a water gate or drainage outlet, paraphrased as mizzu cado. The Portuguese begins a description of a passage or channel, with pera divided at the line end.
The passage carries water out. The article is as, with the short final s weak in the scan; the OCR's ar would not give the visible plural article.

The entry gives Suimono and prefers the alternative Soimono. Sacana, a Japanese food term embedded in the Portuguese definition, introduces the dish described below. The damaged headword is read with its remaining minims and the food explanation; Potiùs is the chosen Latin label, with its small i partly obscured by uneven ink and show-through.

runs.text: ſe dà cozida com caldo pera fazer beber vi-

lines.note: The dish is served cooked with broth to encourage drinking wine. The physical division vi-nho is preserved instead of moving text between rows.
This completes vinho and adds the alternative purpose of hospitality or welcoming treatment. Agaſalhado is kept as printed rather than normalized to another Portuguese form.

Suimu is a dream seen while sleeping. The headword has m rather than the OCR's ni. Enlargement shows a short descending accent stroke over e in vè, retained as a grave rather than the OCR's tilde or a modernized circumflex.
Suinan denotes trouble or loss caused by water, explicitly mizzuno nangui. The final n of the headword and the doubled z in the paraphrase are supported by the scan; perda continues below.
This completes perda and specifies water as the cause. The line belongs to the water-related calamity entry rather than the following entry about age.
Suinen denotes declining years, paraphrased as votoroyuru toxi. No clear stop is printed between the headword and the paraphrase, so none is supplied.
The years or age are described as progressively weakening. This completes the preceding Japanese expression for declining age.
Suinô is a strainer, with mizzucoxi as the Japanese equivalent. The Portuguese first describes a cloth for filtering water and then introduces a second physical form.

runs.text: coadouro feito à maneira de vaſo.

lines.note: The second form is a vessel-shaped strainer. The Portuguese complements the cloth strainer in the preceding row and does not introduce another entry.
Suiqi is the vapor or quality of water, paraphrased as mizzuno qi. The scan includes the i in qualidade that was absent from the draft.
The second gloss is an unseen or hidden quality of water. The joined dagoa is retained as the printed historical form.

Suiqiǒ denotes drunkenness or disorder through intoxication, with yoi gurui as the Japanese paraphrase. The vowel in deſordem is o, not the OCR's a, and q̃ abbreviates the relative pronoun continued below.
The disorder results from excessive drinking, and Suiqio ſuru supplies the verbal construction. The example lacks the headword's length mark in this printing and is retained that way.
A different Suiqio concerns praising or extolling, paraphrased as fuqi aguru. The nasal abbreviation and the physical division engrãde-cer are preserved.
This completes the explanation of praising and magnifying something. The line belongs to Suiqio in the sense of commendation, not the neighboring drunkenness entries.
Suiqiǒjin is a drunkard who causes disturbances and behaves irrationally. The scan supports Bebado rather than Pebado; the last word continues as de-ſatinos.
This completes deſatinos and attributes the irrational acts to drunkenness. The hyphenation belongs to the physical page and is not collapsed in the transcription.
Suiqua combines water and fire. The example begins here and continues both into the following physical row and beyond this page.

The Japanese says not to make the vessels for fire and water one and the same. The continuation reads çuamonouo with a single u before a, rather than the OCR's çuuamonouo; the Portuguese stops after 'fire, and,' with agoa supplied only as the separate catchword below.
